name: Uma Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my aunt Rosa and uncle Felipe on their farm up past the quarry road, about forty hectares. It's apples and pears, a hundred and twenty dairy goats, and a small cheese room where we make a soft cheese for the market and two shops in town. I do the goat milking morning and evening and help in the cheese room, and from August to October it's picking, picking, picking. Ten years I've been there, since I left school for the agriculture course.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cheese room, it's quiet and it smells good and I know exactly what I'm doing in there. What wears me out is picking season, my shoulders, and the fact that family pay is family pay, which means low. I live with Ruben, he's a mechanic at the garage in the village, and we've got a couple of weeks saved if nothing breaks. I don't use any of the AI things, I've got a phone for calls and the weather and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Well, there's been plenty of that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it's like everything else, a lot of noise and then it settles. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post. At the market I'd probably agree with whoever brought it up and then talk about the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me, and I'm fine with that. Goats need milking whether a computer is clever or not. The cheese doesn't care what's on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, milking, cheese, picking. I'd keep trying to put a little aside, though a little is all it ever is. I wouldn't try any of the AI apps, I've no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing that could go wrong for you in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad frost in April, or the goats getting sick. Two years ago we lost half the pear blossom to frost and Felipe had to cut my hours for the winter. That's the kind of thing I actually worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you and Ruben manage that winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruben did extra Saturdays at the garage and I did some cleaning for a holiday cottage. It was tight but we managed. That's sort of how I think about everything, you get through it.

S0.say: It's like everything else: lots of noise, then it settles. She wouldn't post anything and would steer conversations at the market back to the weather.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her and she's fine with that. Goats need milking and cheese needs making regardless of the news.
S0.do: Keeps milking, making cheese and picking as usual. Tries to save a little and doesn't touch AI apps.
S0.quote: The cheese doesn't care what's on the news.
S0.fieldNote: Uma's real worries are frost and goat health, and she has lived through a lean winter already. Her approach is to get through hard patches with extra shifts and odd jobs. She is quiet in public and avoids taking sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs changing. Hm. Not goats, surely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good and bad in it and we'll have to see. If someone asked at the market, I'd say small farms like ours will be fine because people want real cheese. I'd keep it middle of the road, that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think picking is the bit that goes. If there's a machine that picks apples cheaper than seasonal workers and me, Felipe would hire it for the season, he's practical. I'd keep the goats and lose the autumn, and the autumn is a third of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the machines actually do, I wouldn't rush into anything. If my autumn hours went, I'd look for cleaning or shop work in town for those months. I'd ask Rosa to let me do more in the cheese room to make up some of the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my mind but it's not here yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run a picking machine if Felipe got one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. Ruben's the one for machines. I'd probably let him show Felipe how it works and I'd stay with the goats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would decide how these changes go, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarkets mostly, they set the prices. And the government a bit. I don't really blame anyone, it's just how markets go, but it's never the small farms making the decisions.

S1.say: There's good and bad in it, and small farms will be fine because people want real cheese. She'd keep her views middle of the road.
S1.think: Apple picking would likely be automated, taking about a third of her yearly pay. She'd keep the goats but lose the autumn work.
S1.do: Waits to see what the machines actually do. Looks for cleaning or shop work in town in autumn if her picking hours go, and asks for more cheese room work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry in the back of her mind.
S1.quote: I'd keep the goats and lose the autumn, and the autumn is a third of my pay.
S1.fieldNote: Uma quickly pins the risk to one season and one share of her income. She avoids learning the machines and hands that role to her partner without hesitation. She sees supermarkets and markets as the deciders but doesn't really blame anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's two harvests. That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to calm down and governments need to do something sensible, help people through it. I'd say it reasonably, I don't shout. If there was a meeting at the village hall about it, I'd go and listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it would be very bad for us. If robots can milk goats and pick apples, the big farms will do it all for nothing, and Felipe and Rosa couldn't compete on price. Ruben's garage would get the robot cars and robot repairs. We'd both be out within a year, and I don't know anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on everything except food and rent, straight away. I'd go and ask Rosa and Felipe straight what they'd do, and if the farm was going under, I'd ask my mum if we could stay with her for a while. I'd look for any work in town, but I don't know what there'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know anything else. What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shop work, I suppose, or cleaning, like that winter. But if robots can milk a goat they can stack a shelf. That's the bit I can't get round: every back-up job I've ever had is something a robot could do too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools then, if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to. I don't want to, and I wouldn't know where to start. I'd ask Ruben's sister, she uses them for her job, and I'd feel stupid asking.

S2.say: People need to stay calm and governments need to help people through it sensibly. She'd attend a village hall meeting to listen.
S2.think: The family farm couldn't compete with robot-run farms, and her partner's garage would also suffer. Both could be out of work within a year with nothing else she knows.
S2.do: Cuts spending to food and rent straight away. Asks her aunt and uncle about the farm's future and her mother about moving in. Looks for shop or cleaning work in town.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick, aware that every backup job she has is also at risk.
S2.quote: That's the bit I can't get round: every back-up job I've ever had is something a robot could do too.
S2.fieldNote: Her usual way of getting through, picking up odd jobs, stops working here, and she sees that clearly. She'd reluctantly learn AI tools but feels embarrassed to ask for help. Family is her first and last safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but at least it's a few harvests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, let's be sensible, let the government work out support for people like us. I'd probably say we'd adapt like farmers always do, even if I didn't fully believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to feel it coming and not do enough about it. That's how I'd be, I know myself. I'd keep saying next year, next year, until the robot was in the orchard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save something, maybe thirty a month, more if Ruben got more hours. I'd talk to Rosa about whether the cheese could be sold as handmade, so people pay extra for it being made by a person. Mostly I'd keep working and keep an eye on what the other farms did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not sick like the two-year one, but a steady worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would people pay more for cheese made by a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's made by a person, same reason people buy bread from the bakery and not the supermarket. Some people would, not everyone. It might be enough to keep the cheese room going, if not the orchard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep saying next year. What would actually make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Felipe telling me he was cutting my hours. That's what it took last time. I don't move until something pushes me.

S3.say: Let's be sensible and let the government work out support. Farmers always adapt, she'd say, even if she didn't fully believe it.
S3.think: Five years is enough to see it coming but she knows she'd keep putting off acting. She'd only move when pushed, as before.
S3.do: Saves about thirty a month. Asks her aunt about selling the cheese as handmade at a higher price. Keeps working and watches what other farms do.
S3.feel: Anxious, a steady worry rather than sickness.
S3.quote: I'd keep saying next year, next year, until the robot was in the orchard.
S3.fieldNote: Uma is strikingly honest about her own delay: she knows she'd say next year until it's too late. Her one idea is to sell human-made cheese at a premium. She admits it takes a cut in hours to make her act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Rosa and Felipe would be nearly seventy by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen, let's not get ahead of ourselves. I'd say it calmly and mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think in ten years I'd probably be running the cheese room myself, because Rosa can't do it forever. If we sold it as handmade cheese, there might be a small business there that a robot doesn't take, because the point is a person made it. The orchard and the goats would probably go to machines, or get sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn more of the cheese side from Rosa, properly, the recipes and the selling. In a few years I might do a short course on running a small food business, the college does one. I'd keep saving the thirty a month and keep going at the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a version of this where I'm alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools for that business, the selling side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Ruben would do that bit. I'd make the cheese. I'm not against it, I just don't want my hands anywhere near it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether there's a farm left to take over. In two years the farm goes before Rosa retires. In ten, I might get the cheese room, and that's a real job I'd like.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, so let's not get ahead of ourselves. She'd say it calmly and mostly mean it.
S4.think: In ten years she might be running her aunt's cheese room, selling handmade cheese that a robot wouldn't replace. The orchard and goats would probably go to machines or be sold.
S4.do: Learns the cheese recipes and selling from her aunt. Takes a short college course on running a small food business in a few years. Saves about thirty a month and keeps working.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but she can see a version where she's alright.
S4.quote: In ten, I might get the cheese room, and that's a real job I'd like.
S4.fieldNote: For Uma, time decides whether there's a family business left to take over. Her idea of a human-made niche is the one bright spot in all five pictures. She'd leave the tech side to her partner, which she said without apology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Ruben and I both out, and every back-up job gone too. What would help is the government paying people a wage for a while so they're not on the street, and help for small farms to keep going, maybe for selling things that are made by people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about family. On a family farm, if it goes, it's not just a job, it's Christmas dinners and who talks to who. I'd hate to be the one who watched Felipe sell it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against it, I just don't want my hands anywhere near it.
portrait: Uma Torres is 27 and has worked for ten years on her aunt and uncle's orchard and dairy goat farm, milking, picking and making cheese. She lives with her partner Ruben, a village mechanic, with a couple of weeks of savings, and never uses AI tools. Pragmatic and middle of the road, she blames markets more than people. She's calm at a plateau, uneasy at steady change because apple picking could go, and alarmed at AGI in two years when every backup job seems at risk. With ten years she sees a hopeful path running the cheese room and selling cheese made by a person, though she admits she rarely acts until pushed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Ruben would both lose work at once and every backup job she knows would also be automated.
whatWouldHelp: A temporary wage from the government so people don't lose their homes, and help for small farms, perhaps for selling things made by people.
